findings.claim: "During the Lower Palaeozoic (Cambrian to Devonian, roughly 540–360 million years ago), what is now Britain sat in the southern hemisphere tropics or subtropics"
findings.truth: The Lower (Early) Palaeozoic is the Cambrian, Ordovician and Silurian, roughly 540–420 Ma; the Devonian is Upper Palaeozoic. Britain was also not tropical throughout: Avalonia lay at high southern latitudes (~60°S) in the Cambrian and drifted north into the subtropics by the Silurian.
findings.evidence: Standard stratigraphic division of the Palaeozoic (ICS chart: Silurian ends 419.2 Ma); spec 2.4c asks for latitude change 'from the Lower Palaeozoic to the Cenozoic', so the term must be used correctly.

findings.claim: Q5 stem: "A geologist finds a sequence of rocks in Wales that includes Carboniferous Limestone overlain by Carboniferous tillite." Mark scheme: "cross-cutting relationships show the change was from warmer to colder, linking to the southward position of Gondwana".
findings.truth: There is no Carboniferous tillite in Wales. In the Carboniferous the British area sat on or near the equator (the lesson itself says so) and Carboniferous Limestone is overlain by Millstone Grit and Coal Measures, not glacial deposits. The Carboniferous–Permian tillites are on the Gondwanan continents (southern Africa, South America, India, Australia). The principle that dates a limestone–tillite sequence is superposition, not cross-cutting relationships.
findings.evidence: Spec 2.4a (Carboniferous tillites deposited close to the equator on drifted continents); lesson L1 n11 states Britain lay near the equator in the Carboniferous; internal contradiction.

findings.claim: "By about 6,500 years ago, Britain had become an island." (repeated in flashcard 6)
findings.truth: Britain was cut off from continental Europe by about 6500 BCE, i.e. roughly 8,500 years ago. 6,500 years ago (4500 BCE) is a BC-to-BP conversion error; the Dogger Bank itself survived as an island until at least 5000 BCE.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Doggerland: 'cutting off what was previously the British peninsula from the European mainland by around 6500 BCE'.

findings.claim: "During the Last Glacial Maximum around 20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered ... Britain north of the Thames–Severn line."
findings.truth: The Thames line is the Anglian limit (about 450,000 years ago), the furthest south ice ever reached in Britain. At the Devensian Last Glacial Maximum the ice front lay far to the north, roughly across Norfolk, the Midlands and south Wales.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Anglian stage: 'in the London area the ice sheet reached as far south as Hornchurch and Finchley ... the furthest south the ice reached in any Pleistocene ice age'.

findings.claim: "Examiners regularly ask students to explain the mechanism behind sea level change"
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners do. House rule: describe the exam in neutral terms, never assert examiner behaviour or reward.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: fabricated examiner claims are a FIX.

findings.claim: "the stomatal density of fossil leaves (fewer stomata open when CO2 is high)"
findings.truth: Stomatal density is about how many stomata a leaf grows, not how many are open. Leaves that develop under high CO2 grow fewer stomata per unit area; opening and closing is a separate, short-term response.
findings.evidence: Standard stomatal-density CO2 proxy method (Woodward 1987 and later palaeobotanical use).

findings.claim: "The dark lunar maria (plains) are filled with basaltic lava from later volcanic eruptions between about 3 and 1 billion years ago." (repeated in flashcard 5)
findings.truth: Most mare basalts erupted between about 3.5 and 3.0 billion years ago, with the phase usually given as roughly 3.9–3.0 Ga; only rare late flows are as young as 2.0–1.2 Ga. Starting the range at 3 Ga leaves out the main phase, and L5 of this same unit gives 3.9–3.0 Ga, so the two lessons contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Lunar mare: 'the majority of mare basalts appear to have erupted between about 3 and 3.5 Ga'; oldest 4.2 Ga, youngest ~2.03 Ga (Chang'e-5) to ~1.2 Ga by crater counting.

findings.claim: "Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km tall — nearly three times the height of Mauna Kea from its ocean base."
findings.truth: Mauna Kea rises about 10.2 km from its base on the ocean floor, so 22 km is a little over twice that height, not nearly three times.
findings.evidence: Recomputation: 22 / 10.2 = 2.2. Mauna Kea summit 4,207 m above sea level, base about 6,000 m below sea level.

findings.claim: "Examiners regularly ask students to explain this difference" (content) and "Examiners also penalise answers that say Olympus Mons is big because Mars is big" (exam tip)
findings.truth: Both are invented claims about examiner behaviour and marking. The teaching point is sound; only the attribution to examiners must go.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: fabricated examiner claims are a FIX.

findings.claim: "Apollo lunar samples, radiocarbon-dated using radiometric methods, have calibrated the crater count chronology for the Moon"
findings.truth: Apollo samples were dated by long-lived radiometric systems (K-Ar / Ar-Ar, Rb-Sr, U-Pb). Radiocarbon dates organic carbon and reaches back only about 50,000 years, so it cannot date lunar basalts billions of years old. The phrase is also self-contradictory.
findings.evidence: Radiocarbon half-life 5,730 years, practical limit ~50 ka; lunar chronology is built on Ar-Ar and Rb-Sr ages of Apollo and Luna samples.

findings.claim: "For Jezero Crater, the key examiner point is that the delta deposits suggest ancient liquid water"
findings.truth: An invented appeal to examiner priorities. The geology is right; state it as the key point.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: fabricated examiner claims are a FIX.

findings.claim: Q5 stem tells the student to "Use the principle of superposition" but describes two craters that merely sit side by side ("a neighbouring crater"), with no overlap; the mark scheme then awards a mark for "applying superposition".
findings.truth: Superposition needs one feature to lie on or cut another. Two options: (a) reword the stem so the fresh crater's ejecta rays lie across the degraded crater, which makes superposition genuinely usable and keeps all four mark points; or (b) drop 'superposition' from the stem and the mark scheme and mark it purely on state of preservation. Recommendation: option (a) — it is the smaller change and keeps the spec skill of relative dating on planetary surfaces.
findings.evidence: Recomputation of the mark scheme against the stem; lesson n10 defines superposition correctly as one crater sitting on top of another.
findings.ruling: Stem reworded so the rays overlie the older crater.

findings.claim: "Ice cores — drilled from Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets — ... showing values between 180 ppm (ice ages) and 280 ppm (interglacials) over the past 800,000 years."
findings.truth: The 800,000-year CO2 record is Antarctic only (EPICA Dome C). Greenland cores reach about 130,000 years and their CO2 is unreliable because of dust reactions. The body text says 'Antarctic' correctly; only the takeaway blurs the two.
findings.evidence: EPICA Dome C 800 ka record; NGRIP/GISP2 Greenland cores ~123–130 ka.

findings.claim: Q2 asks two things ("Name the ... crater and state the main geological reason for its selection") but is labelled 1 mark, and the scheme says 'accept either part alone for 1 mark'.
findings.truth: The stem demands two responses for one mark. Not wrong on facts; a mark-allocation mismatch only.
findings.evidence: Internal inconsistency between stem, type label and mark scheme.

findings.claim: "Watch out for questions that ask you to distinguish eustatic sea level change from isostatic (land level) change — these are tested separately."
findings.truth: Nothing in the specification says the two are tested separately; the on-screen paper draws on the whole content and can combine them. The advice to distinguish them is good; the claim about how they are tested is invented but harmless in isolation.
findings.evidence: Spec summary of assessment: the on-screen paper covers all subject content with data and stimulus response questions.

summary: Eleven FIX findings across all five lessons: three HIGH (Lower Palaeozoic defined as Cambrian-Devonian; a Carboniferous tillite invented in Wales, contradicting the lesson's own equatorial Britain; Apollo samples described as radiocarbon-dated), plus a BC-to-BP slip on Doggerland, the Anglian ice limit given as the Last Glacial Maximum limit, wrong mare-basalt ages, a Mauna Kea ratio and four fabricated examiner claims. One ADJUDICATE (a superposition question with nothing to superpose) and three NOTEs.
